content.text: System.Text.Json isn't Newtonsoft.Json with a faster engine. It's strict where Newtonsoft guesses, it writes the properties of the declared type rather than the runtime type, and outside ASP.NET Core's own settings it uses PascalCase and escapes every non-ASCII character. Switching serializers changes your API's contract unless you configure those differences on purpose.

The belief: System.Text.Json is a drop-in replacement for Newtonsoft.Json. Same job, same API shape,
, so the same objects produce the same JSON.

There's a lot behind that belief. For simple DTOs, the output really is identical. ASP.NET Core already hides the most visible differences: it configures camelCase names, case-insensitive matching and numbers in quotes. And Microsoft's migration guide has a table where most Newtonsoft features get a check mark on the System.Text.Json side.

Read that table closely, though. Many check marks point to an attribute or a setting you have to add, not to a default. The guide states the design difference directly: System.Text.Json is strict by default and avoids guessing, for performance and security; Newtonsoft.Json is flexible by default.
